title: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
summary: How extra compute per prompt improves LLM answers: pass@k coverage, majority vote and best-of-N, PRM-guided search, compute-optimal allocation, reasoning models with budget forcing, and when it beats a bigger model.
outcomes: Compute pass@k from a per-sample success rate and with the unbiased estimator from n samples
Explain why majority vote and reward models plateau while coverage keeps rising
Choose between best-of-N, PRM beam search and sequential revisions based on prompt difficulty
Explain how reasoning models and s1 budget forcing turn thinking tokens into accuracy, and where it stops
Compute the FLOPs-matched test-time budget versus a larger model and judge which is better

lessons.title: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt

blocks.md: Scaling laws describe how loss falls as you spend more **training** compute: more parameters, more tokens. But once a model is trained, we usually let it answer each prompt **once**, with one pass of decoding. **Test-time compute** (also called inference-time compute) is everything extra you spend on a single prompt after training: more samples, longer reasoning, or a search guided by a scorer.

Why would that help? A model that answers a hard math problem correctly 20% of the time already *contains* the solution in its output distribution. One greedy answer throws that away. Sampling many times, thinking longer, or revising can recover it. The question this course answers is how far that goes and how to spend the extra compute well.

Snell et al. (UC Berkeley and Google DeepMind, 2024) give a useful frame. Test-time methods have two parts:

- a **proposer**: the LLM's distribution over answers, which you can improve at test time (for example by asking it to revise its own previous attempts), and
- a **verifier**: anything that scores or selects among candidates (unit tests, a proof checker, a majority vote, an outcome reward model, or a process reward model).

The s1 paper (Muennighoff et al., 2025), citing Snell et al. and Brown et al., names a second split: **parallel** methods run independent attempts (best-of-N, majority voting), while **sequential** methods let later computation build on earlier computation (a longer chain of thought, revisions).

blocks.title: Proposer and verifier, parallel and sequential

scenes.caption: The default: one prompt, one pass through the model, one answer. All the model's other possible answers are never seen.
Parallel scaling: draw N independent samples at positive temperature. They can explore different approaches, but none of them learns from the others.
A verifier turns many samples into one answer. Its quality decides whether the extra samples help at all.
Sequential scaling: each new attempt conditions on the previous ones (a revision, or simply more chain of thought), so it can fix a mistake instead of starting over.
Snell et al. mix both: some budget on parallel chains, some on revising within each chain, with the verifier picking within and across chains.

blocks.md: To compare methods fairly we need a unit of cost. Papers usually count **generations** (one full sampled answer), **tokens**, or **FLOPs**. A rough rule from the scaling-laws literature, used by Snell et al., is that generating $D$ tokens with an $N$-parameter dense model costs about $2ND$ FLOPs, while training on $D$ tokens costs about $6ND$. We return to that exchange rate in the last lesson.

Test-time scaling has two halves that can fail independently. **Coverage**: does any attempt contain a correct answer? **Precision**: can you pick it out? The next two lessons take them one at a time.

Test-time compute is not free at serving time. Every extra sample or thinking token is paid on every request, by every user. Training compute is paid once. That asymmetry decides when test-time scaling is worth it.

blocks.question: A team samples 16 answers per question from a fixed model and keeps the one their reward model scores highest. In the proposer/verifier frame, what are they changing?
options: Only the verifier side: the proposal distribution is the same model sampled 16 times
Only the proposer: more samples means a better model
Both, because sampling at temperature changes the model's weights
Neither: this is training-time compute
blocks.explain: Best-of-N leaves the proposer untouched; each of the 16 samples comes from the same distribution. All the gain comes from selecting among them with a verifier. Changing the proposer means, for example, conditioning on previous attempts (revisions) or a longer reasoning trace.

blocks.question: Which method is **sequential** in the s1 paper's sense?
options: Majority vote over 64 independent samples
Best-of-N with unit tests
Letting the model keep reasoning after it tried to stop, so later tokens build on earlier ones
Running the same prompt on 8 GPUs at once
blocks.explain: Sequential means later computation depends on earlier computation, like a longer chain of thought or a revision. The other options are independent attempts (parallel) or just hardware parallelism.

lessons.title: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples

blocks.md: Start with one problem. Suppose each independent sample is correct with probability $p$ (the model's **per-sample success rate**, also called pass@1 for that problem). If we draw $k$ samples, the chance that **at least one** is correct is one minus the chance that all $k$ fail.

blocks.caption: Assumes the k samples are independent draws with the same success rate p.

blocks.md: A tiny example. With $p = 0.05$: one sample succeeds 5% of the time, 10 samples succeed $1 - 0.95^{10} = 40.1\%$ of the time, 50 samples 92.3%, and 100 samples 99.4%. You need 45 samples to pass 90%. A model that looks useless with one shot can be very useful if something can check its answers.

blocks.title: pass@k for one problem with per-sample success rate p

scenes.caption: p = 0.05: 5% at k = 1, 40.1% at k = 10, 99.4% at k = 100. On a log x-axis each curve is an S shape.
An easier problem (p = 0.3) saturates by k of about 10. A harder one (p = 0.02) needs about 100 samples to reach 87%.
Drag p. Every curve has the same shape, just shifted left or right on the log axis: halving p roughly doubles the k needed.

blocks.md: A benchmark is many problems with very different $p$. **Coverage** (Brown et al., 2024, *Large Language Monkeys*) is the fraction of problems solved by at least one of $k$ samples: the average of pass@k over problems. Averaging S-curves with offsets spread over orders of magnitude gives a curve that rises steadily over many decades of $k$.

scenes.caption: At k = 1 coverage is just mean p: (0.5 + 0.1 + 0.01 + 0.001) / 4 = 0.153.
Each 10x more samples unlocks the next harder problem: 0.439, then 0.682. The easy problem is already solved and stops contributing.
0.908 at 1,000 and 1.0 at 10,000. Gains per decade stay roughly steady (0.29, 0.24, 0.23) until the last problem is solved: this is why real coverage curves look log-linear over orders of magnitude.

blocks.md: Brown et al. measured this with up to 10,000 samples per problem. On SWE-bench Lite (real GitHub issues checked by unit tests), DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct solved 15.9% of issues with one sample and 56% with 250, above the 43% single-attempt state of the art at the time. On CodeContests, Gemma-2B went from 0.02% to 7.1% coverage at 10,000 samples. They fit coverage $c$ with an **exponentiated power law** in the number of samples $k$:

blocks.caption: Brown et al., eq. 3. For Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH they report a = -1.33, b = -0.43.

blocks.title: Fitted coverage law, Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH

scenes.caption: With the paper's fit, k = 100 gives 83.2% (the paper measured 82.9%) and k = 10,000 gives 97.5% (measured 98.44%).
A more negative a shifts the curve right (a weaker model needs more samples). Here a = -3.88, b = -0.11, the paper's Llama-3-8B-Instruct CodeContests fit, which climbs far more slowly.

blocks.md: When you estimate pass@k from data, do not compute $1 - (1 - \hat p)^k$ from the observed rate, and do not draw just $k$ samples once (high variance). Chen et al. (2021, the Codex paper) draw $n \ge k$ samples, count $c$ correct, and use the unbiased estimator below, the probability that a random size-$k$ subset of the $n$ samples contains at least one correct one. Brown et al. use the same formula.

blocks.title: The numerically stable estimator from the Codex paper

scenes.caption: 10 samples, 3 correct, and we ask for pass@2.
There are 7 wrong samples, at least k = 2, so some 2-subsets can be all wrong. No early return.
The product telescopes to C(7,2)/C(10,2) = 21/45 without computing large binomials: (1 - 2/8)(1 - 2/9)(1 - 2/10) = 0.75 x 0.778 x 0.8 = 0.467.
pass@2 = 0.533. The plug-in formula 1 - 0.7^2 = 0.51 gives a different number: the estimator counts subsets of the samples you actually drew.

blocks.prompt: Same data, n = 10 and c = 3. What does the estimator give for pass@5, and how does it compare with $1 - 0.7^5$?
blocks.reveal: $1 - \binom{7}{5}/\binom{10}{5} = 1 - 21/252 = 0.917$, while $1 - 0.7^5 = 0.832$. With only 7 wrong samples, most 5-subsets must contain a correct one. The estimator is unbiased for any $n \ge k$; drawing $n$ much larger than $k$ only lowers its variance. The Codex paper used $n = 200$ for $k \le 100$ and averaged over problems.

blocks.md: Coverage is an **upper bound** on accuracy. It equals real accuracy only if you have a perfect checker (unit tests, a proof checker). For a math word problem, pass@100 = 83% means 83% of problems have *some* correct sample, not that you can find it.

blocks.question: A model has pass@1 = 0.01 on a problem. Roughly how many independent samples give a 63% chance of at least one correct answer?
options: About 10
About 63
About 100
About 1,000
blocks.explain: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. In general, $k \approx 1/p$ samples give about $1 - 1/e = 63\%$ coverage for small $p$.

blocks.question: Brown et al. find coverage on many tasks grows roughly log-linearly with k over several orders of magnitude. What best explains that shape?
options: Samples from an LLM become more accurate as you draw more of them
The benchmark mixes problems whose per-sample success rates span many orders of magnitude, so each 10x in k unlocks another slice
Temperature is raised automatically as k grows
pass@k for a single problem is linear in log k
blocks.explain: For one problem, pass@k is a sharp S-curve in log k. Averaging many such curves with offsets spread across decades smooths them into a steady rise. Samples are independent and do not get better individually.

lessons.title: Precision: majority vote, best-of-N and when they plateau

blocks.md:
Without an automatic checker, you must choose one answer from $N$ samples. Three standard rules:

1. **Majority vote** (self-consistency, Wang et al., 2022): parse each sample's final answer and return the most common one.
2. **Best-of-N**: score every sample with a reward model and return the top-scoring sample's answer.
3. **Weighted best-of-N**: add up reward scores for samples that share a final answer and return the answer with the largest total (used by Snell et al., following Li et al.).

Self-consistency sampled 40 reasoning paths and, on PaLM-540B, improved chain-of-thought accuracy on GSM8K by 17.9 points over greedy decoding.

Let us run all three rules on the same 8 samples for one problem whose correct answer is 15. Each sample has a final answer and a verifier score in [0, 1] (the score is an illustrative number, not from a real model).

blocks.title: Eight samples, three selection rules (toy scores)

scenes.caption: Eight samples. The correct answer, 15, appears twice. Wrong answer 12 appears three times.
Majority vote counts answers: 12 has 3 votes, 15 and 18 have 2, 20 has 1. It returns 12: wrong, because a wrong answer is the plurality.
Best-of-N returns the single top score, 0.92, whose answer is 20: wrong. One overconfident score decides everything.
Weighted best-of-N sums scores per answer: 15 gets 0.85 + 0.80 = 1.65, 12 gets 1.20, 20 gets 0.92, 18 gets 0.30. It returns 15: correct.

blocks.md: Weighted voting combines two weak signals: how often the model reaches an answer and how much the verifier likes it. Snell et al. adopt it, following Li et al., as the final selection step in all their PRM search experiments.

Now ask what happens as $N$ grows. Majority vote converges to whichever answer has the largest probability under the model. If the correct answer is the **mode** of the model's answer distribution, accuracy climbs toward 100%. If a wrong answer is the mode, accuracy falls toward 0%, even though coverage rises to 100%. Here are exact numbers for two toy problems (ties broken at random).

blocks.prompt: Problem B: the model answers correctly with probability 0.2 and gives one particular wrong answer with probability 0.5 (the rest is split between two other wrong answers, 0.15 each). What happens to majority-vote accuracy as N goes from 1 to 64?
blocks.reveal: It **falls**: 0.20 at N = 1, 0.159 at N = 4, 0.059 at N = 16, and 0.001 at N = 64. Meanwhile coverage $1 - 0.8^N$ rises to 0.59, 0.97 and essentially 1.0. More samples make the vote more confident in the model's favorite wrong answer.

blocks.title: Majority vote vs coverage as N grows (exact, toy distributions)

scenes.caption: Problem A: correct answer has probability 0.4, wrong ones 0.3, 0.2, 0.1. Correct is the mode, so majority accuracy rises: 0.40, 0.47, 0.63, 0.83.
Problem B: correct 0.2, one wrong answer 0.5. The wrong answer is the mode, so majority accuracy drops: 0.20, 0.16, 0.06, 0.001.
Coverage on problem B over the same N: 0.20, 0.59, 0.97, 1.00. The correct answer is almost surely in the pool; voting just cannot find it.

blocks.md: This is exactly what Brown et al. observed at scale. With Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH, coverage rose from 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote and reward-model selection only moved from 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. All three selection methods plateaued around 100 samples. Rare correct answers, sampled 1% of the time or less, are a needle in a haystack that a vote cannot find and an imperfect reward model often misses.

Reward models have a second failure: **over-optimization**. The harder you search for a high score, the more you find samples that exploit the verifier's mistakes rather than samples that are correct. Snell et al. saw this with PRM-guided search on easy questions (next lesson). Even unit tests are imperfect: Brown et al. found flaky test suites in 11.3% of SWE-bench Lite problems.
Repeated sampling scales **coverage** smoothly; selection without a reliable checker does not keep up. The useful question is never only how many samples, but how good is the verifier at the tail.

blocks.question: Your majority-vote accuracy on a math benchmark stops improving between N = 64 and N = 512, but pass@512 (checked against the answer key) keeps rising. What is the most likely reason?
options: Samples become correlated at large N
On the unsolved problems the correct answer is a minority answer, so adding votes reinforces the wrong mode
The model runs out of context window
pass@k is computed incorrectly at large N
blocks.explain: Majority vote converges to the mode of the answer distribution. For problems where a wrong answer is the mode, more samples raise coverage but not voting accuracy. That is the plateau Brown et al. report.

blocks.question: With the eight toy samples above, which rule would change its answer if sample 4 (answer 20, score 0.92) were removed?
options: Majority vote
Weighted best-of-N
Best-of-N
All three
blocks.explain: Best-of-N would switch to the next-highest score, 0.85, whose answer is 15. Majority vote still picks 12 (3 votes) and weighted best-of-N still picks 15 (1.65 vs 1.20).

lessons.title: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation

blocks.md:
A process reward model (PRM) scores every **step** of a solution, not just the final answer. Best-of-N only uses the PRM at the end. With step scores we can **prune** bad partial solutions early and spend the budget on promising ones. Snell et al. compare three ways to search against a PRM, all at the same *generation budget* $N$:

- **Best-of-N weighted**: sample $N$ full solutions, score each by the PRM's prediction at its last step, aggregate per answer.
- **Beam search**: keep $N$ candidates; after each step keep the top $N/M$ by PRM score and expand each into $M$ new next steps.
- **Lookahead search**: beam search, but score each step by rolling it out $k$ more steps greedily and using the PRM at the end of the rollout. It costs $N \times (k+1)$ samples.

blocks.title: Beam search with N = 4 candidates, M = 2 (toy PRM scores)

scenes.caption: Sample N = 4 different first steps and score each with the PRM.
Keep the top N/M = 2 (A and C). B and D are dropped after one step instead of being completed, which is where the savings come from.
Expand each survivor into M = 2 next steps: back to 4 candidates. Score again and keep A1 (.66) and C2 (.80).
Repeat until solutions finish (Snell et al. cap it at 40 rounds). Step 3 shows the children of A1 (.70, .58) and C2 (.83, .31). The finished candidates then go through weighted best-of-N.

blocks.md: What did they find on MATH with PaLM 2-S*? At small budgets beam search clearly beat best-of-N. As the budget grew the advantage shrank and beam search often fell **below** best-of-N. Lookahead search, the most thorough optimizer, generally did worst at equal budget. Inspecting outputs showed the search exploiting the PRM: repetitive low-information steps, or suspiciously short 1 to 2 step solutions.

Splitting the test set by **difficulty** explains it. Snell et al. define difficulty relative to the model: estimate each question's pass@1 from 2048 samples and bin questions into five quantiles (level 1 easiest). On easy levels 1 and 2, beam search **degraded** with more budget, amplifying the PRM's spurious features where the model was already mostly right. On levels 3 and 4, beam search consistently beat best-of-N, because there the model rarely samples a correct answer without guidance. On level 5 no method made much progress.

blocks.title: A compute-optimal router (simplified from Snell et al.)

nodes.label:
Medium bins:
PRM beam search,
seq/parallel mix

Hardest bin:
little gain from
test-time compute

scenes.caption: The compute-optimal strategy picks the test-time hyperparameters (search method, beam width, sequential vs parallel ratio) per prompt, using difficulty as the deciding statistic.
In practice difficulty is predicted from the verifier's average score on samples, not from ground truth. The two versions gave largely overlapping curves in the paper.
Easy prompts: the first samples are usually near-right, so local refinement wins and aggressive search risks exploiting the verifier.
Medium prompts: guided search and a balance of parallel exploration with sequential revision pay off most.
Hardest prompts: the paper saw small gains from any method. Here a bigger or better-trained model is the lever.

blocks.md: Snell et al. also changed the **proposer**. They fine-tuned PaLM 2-S* to revise its answer given up to four previous attempts in context. Its pass@1 improved with each revision step, and generating $N$ answers as a sequence of revisions narrowly beat generating $N$ in parallel. But about 38% of correct answers were turned back into incorrect ones by a later revision, so they again used a verifier or majority vote to pick the best answer in each chain. Easy questions did best with all-sequential compute; harder ones with a mix of sequential and parallel.

Choosing the best setting per difficulty bin (on held-out data) is what they call **compute-optimal scaling**. With PRM search it nearly matched best-of-N while using up to 4x less compute (16 versus 64 generations); with revisions it outperformed best-of-N using up to 4x less (64 versus 256). In the discussion they summarize the efficiency gain as 2x to 4x.

These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.
The best use of test-time compute depends on the prompt. Search is most valuable where the model is weak but not hopeless; on easy prompts it can hurt by exploiting the verifier.

blocks.question: Beam search with a PRM beats best-of-N at 16 generations but loses at 256 on easy questions. What is the best explanation?
options: Beam search runs out of beams at large N
With more budget the search finds candidates that score high because of PRM errors, not because they are correct
Best-of-N uses a better reward model
Easy questions need more steps than beam search allows
blocks.explain: This is verifier over-optimization. Snell et al. saw search produce repetitive or overly short solutions that the PRM still scored well. On easy questions best-of-N's weaker optimization pressure is safer.

blocks.question: Lookahead search with k = 3 and N = 16 beams is charged how many generations in Snell et al.'s cost protocol?
blocks.explain: Lookahead costs N x (k + 1) = 16 x 4 = 64, because each step is also rolled out k steps ahead. That extra cost is one reason it underperformed at equal budget.

blocks.question: A product mostly receives easy prompts that the model already solves 70% of the time. Which allocation does the paper's evidence favor?
options: Deep lookahead search against a PRM
Spend the budget sequentially (revise or keep reasoning) rather than on aggressive PRM search
Skip any verifier and return the first sample
Always use the maximum number of parallel samples
blocks.explain: On easy bins, sequential revisions did best and beam search degraded with budget. Light selection (vote or weighted best-of-N) over a revision chain is the safer choice.

lessons.title: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing

blocks.md: The methods so far bolt search onto an ordinary model. Reasoning models move test-time scaling **inside** one generation: the model writes a long chain of thought, checks itself, backtracks, and only then answers. OpenAI's o1 system card states that the o1 series is trained with large-scale reinforcement learning to reason using chain of thought, and that o-series models gain capability by leveraging test-time compute. ChatGPT shows users a summary of that chain of thought rather than the raw text.

DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) published how such behavior can emerge. DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with RL (GRPO, a PPO variant that scores each sampled answer against a group of answers to the same prompt instead of using a value model) from a base model using rule-based rewards (answer correctness and a format that puts reasoning inside `<think>` tags), with no human-written reasoning traces. Over training, its average pass@1 on AIME 2024 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% (86.7% with self-consistency voting), and the average response length grew steadily: the model learned on its own to spend more tokens thinking. The paper also notes that R1 uses fewer tokens on simple tasks and more on complex ones.
Notice the two scaling knobs here. Train-time RL compute makes the model *able* to use long reasoning; test-time tokens are where it *spends* that ability on each prompt.

Can you control how long such a model thinks? **s1** (Muennighoff et al., 2025) shows a very simple recipe. Fine-tune Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on just 1,000 curated questions with reasoning traces (s1K), which took 26 minutes on 16 H100 GPUs. Then apply **budget forcing** at decoding time:

- **Maximum**: if thinking exceeds the budget, append the end-of-thinking delimiter (optionally with "Final Answer:") so the model must answer now.
- **Minimum**: if the model tries to stop early, suppress the end-of-thinking delimiter and append "Wait", which often makes it re-check and fix its answer.

blocks.title: Budget forcing as a decoding loop (simplified)

scenes.caption: Decode the thinking trace one token at a time, as usual.
The model emits end-of-thinking after 900 tokens, but the minimum is 2,000. Instead of stopping, the stop token is dropped and "Wait" is appended.
Thinking continues and the model often re-examines its last step. In the s1 paper's example it recounts and fixes an answer of 2 r's in "raspberry" to 3.
If the trace hits the maximum, thinking is cut and the model is pushed straight to its answer.
Either way the answer is produced after the end-of-thinking delimiter, so test-time compute is controlled exactly by the two budgets.

blocks.md: Results: s1-32B with budget forcing scaled with more thinking tokens. Forcing it to continue (appending "Wait" up to six times) raised AIME24 from 50% to 57%, beyond what it achieved without intervention. The choice of string mattered a little: with 2 forced continuations, "Wait" gave 53.3% on AIME24 versus 50.0% for no string, "Hmm" or "Alternatively". Simply telling the model a token limit in the prompt failed, because the model cannot reliably count tokens; asking for a number of steps was gamed by writing fewer, longer steps.

blocks.prompt: s1 also tried **rejection sampling**: sample until a generation happens to fit a chosen length budget, then use it. If you raise the budget, should accuracy go up like budget forcing?
blocks.reveal: No. The authors found an **inverse** trend: longer accepted generations were less accurate. Their hypothesis: short generations are the ones where the model was on the right track from the start, and long ones are where it made mistakes and backtracked. Length is partly a *symptom* of difficulty, so filtering for length is not the same as granting more thinking.

blocks.md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

Sequential thinking lets later tokens build on earlier ones, which parallel sampling cannot. s1 found that majority voting over the base model could not catch up with the budget-forced fine-tuned model.

blocks.question: You fine-tuned a model like s1 and force 10 extra "Wait" continuations on every hard problem. Accuracy drops compared with 4. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model forgot its fine-tuning
Too many suppressed stops push it into repetitive loops or past the context window, so extra tokens stop adding useful reasoning
Appending "Wait" changes the model's weights
Budget forcing only works on easy problems
blocks.explain: s1 reports that scaling with budget forcing flattens and that suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter too often leads to repetitive loops, while the context window bounds total length.

blocks.question: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's responses became much longer during RL even though no reward term asked for length. Why is that evidence for test-time scaling?
options: Longer outputs are always rewarded by GRPO
Length was capped at 1,000 tokens
The model copied long human traces
The reward was only for correctness and format, so the model discovered that spending more tokens per problem raised its success rate
blocks.explain: R1-Zero's rewards were rule-based accuracy and format rewards. Growth in thinking length alongside accuracy shows the policy learned to buy correctness with test-time tokens.

lessons.title: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model

blocks.md: If extra inference can lift a small model, when is it better than training a bigger one? Snell et al. pose it with FLOPs. A model with $N$ parameters pretrained on $D_{\text{pretrain}}$ tokens costs $X = 6ND_{\text{pretrain}}$, and serving $D_{\text{inference}}$ tokens costs $Y = 2ND_{\text{inference}}$. Multiplying parameters by $M$ (same data) multiplies both, to $M(X+Y)$. To match that total with the small model, its inference compute can grow by a factor

blocks.caption: R is the ratio of inference tokens to pretraining tokens. Derived from X = 6N D_pretrain and Y = 2N D_inference.

blocks.md: Worked example with the paper's $M \approx 14$ (a 14x larger model): at $R = 0.16$ the small model may spend $14 + 3 \cdot 13 / 0.16 = 257.75$ times its baseline inference compute; at $R = 0.79$, 63.4 times; at $R = 22$, only 15.8 times. The more inference traffic you expect relative to pretraining data, the less test-time budget each query gets, because the bigger model's training cost is amortized over many queries.

blocks.title: Test-time budget that matches an M-times larger model

scenes.caption: With M = 14, the three R values Snell et al. tested give 258x, 63x and 16x more inference for the small model.
As R grows the multiplier falls toward M itself: with heavy traffic, the small model can afford barely more than the big model's per-query cost.
Drag M. A smaller gap in size (M = 4) leaves much less room: 60x at R = 0.16, under 5x at R = 22.

blocks.md: Their finding (Figure 9): test-time compute and pretraining are **not 1-to-1 exchangeable**. On easy and medium questions, or when $R$ is small (for example a self-improvement pipeline that generates few tokens), compute-optimal test-time scaling of the small model beat the 14x larger model's greedy answer. On the hardest questions, or with large $R$, scaling parameters was better. Brown et al. saw the same task dependence for repeated sampling: at fixed FLOPs, Llama-3-8B-Instruct reached higher coverage than Llama-3-70B-Instruct on MATH, GSM8K and MiniF2F, while the 70B model was almost always more cost-effective on CodeContests.

FLOPs are not the only cost. Brown et al. note that repeated sampling can run at high batch sizes and use attention optimizations that exploit the shared prompt, so its real throughput is better than FLOPs suggest. Long sequential traces have the opposite problem: tokens come out one after another, which adds latency. Brown et al. also compared API prices on SWE-bench Lite (300 issues) with the same agent framework:

blocks.title: SWE-bench Lite: solve rate and API cost (Brown et al.)

scenes.caption: Issues solved (%): five samples from the cheaper model solve 29.62%, versus 24.00% and 26.70% for one attempt from the frontier models.
Total cost in USD: 5 x 0.0072 x 300 = 10.8, versus 39 and 51. Repeated sampling is 3.6x and 4.7x cheaper here while solving more.

blocks.md:
Putting the course together, a practical checklist:

1. **Is there a reliable checker?** (tests, proof checker, exact answer) Then repeated sampling turns coverage into accuracy, and pass@k guides the budget.
2. **No checker?** Expect majority vote and reward models to plateau; weighted voting and a good PRM help, but beware over-optimization.
3. **Difficulty varies?** Spend adaptively: little on easy prompts, guided search on medium ones, and do not expect miracles on prompts far beyond the model.
4. **Reasoning model?** Control thinking length (budget forcing or the provider's effort settings), and combine with parallel sampling once sequential gains flatten.
5. **Heavy traffic?** A bigger or better-trained model may be cheaper overall than a big per-query test-time budget.
Test-time compute is a second scaling axis, not a replacement for the first. It pays most when the model can already sometimes solve the task and something can recognize a correct answer.

blocks.question: Using Snell et al.'s FLOPs model with M = 14, how much more inference compute can the small model use at R = 1?
A chatbot will serve far more tokens than its pretraining corpus (R much greater than 1), and many prompts are hard for the current model. What does the evidence favor?
options: Investing in a larger or better-trained model
A large per-query test-time budget on the current small model
Majority voting with 10,000 samples
Lookahead search with a PRM
blocks.explain: With large R the FLOPs-matched test-time budget shrinks toward M, and on hard questions Snell et al. found additional pretraining more effective than test-time compute.

blocks.question: Brown et al.'s DeepSeek-Coder setup beat single attempts from GPT-4o and Claude on SWE-bench Lite. Which ingredient made the extra samples convertible into solved issues?
options: A majority vote over patches
A larger context window
A process reward model
The repository's unit tests, which check each candidate automatically
blocks.explain: SWE-bench candidates are checked by the repository's test suite, so higher coverage becomes a higher solve rate directly. Without such a checker, selection plateaus, as lesson 3 showed.
